The Purplegray sculpin Gymnocanthus detrisus exhibits a life-history strategy shaped by the cold, productive waters of the North Pacific. Field surveys conducted in the Bering Sea indicate that the onset of gonadal maturation in females occurs when individuals reach a total length of 18.8 centimeters [Lp = 18.8 centimeters], a size typically attained around three years of age. Males, in contrast, become reproductively active at a slightly smaller body size, with puberty documented at a total length of 17.7 centimeters [Lp = 17.7 centimeters]. This modest sexual dimorphism in maturation size is common among cottids and likely reflects differential energetic investments in gamete production and nest-guarding behavior. The maximum ultimate total length recorded for this species is 36 centimeters [Li = 36 centimeters], though some ichthyological databases report a slightly lower asymptotic size of 29 centimeters for populations in the southern extent of its range; this discrepancy may arise from regional variation in growing season length and prey availability.

At the commencement of exogenous feeding, newly hatched yolk-sac larvae of Gymnocanthus detrisus are exceptionally small, reflecting the high fecundity characteristic of the genus. The wet weight at birth is 0.0023 grams [Wwb = 0.0023 grams], a value derived from the typical egg diameter of related cottids and consistent with an adhesive, demersal egg strategy. This minute prolarval mass imposes a critical window of vulnerability, as the yolk-dependent larva must rapidly develop its mouth gape and retinal differentiation to successfully capture its first prey before exhausting endogenous reserves. The transition to active feeding marks a period of extremely high size-specific mortality, a common bottleneck in the early life history of sculpins. Brood surveys indicate that a single female deposits between 3,000 and 4,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = between 3,000 and 4,000 eggs per spawning event], with the adhesive eggs laid in a compact mass within the nest cavity guarded by the male.

Under the stable thermal conditions typical of the benthic environment where this species resides, approximately 2.9 °C [T = 2.9 °C], the maximum reproductive output is achieved through a well-defined breeding phenology. Females produce a single clutch annually [F_R_i = single clutch annually], each containing approximately 3,000 to 4,000 eggs [N_R_i = each containing approximately 3,000 to 4,000 eggs], a combined expression that results in a total annual fecundity of several thousand eggs per breeding season. This batch-spawning strategy allows the female to incrementally invest in yolk production despite the constraints imposed by low metabolic rates at these temperatures. The mean egg diameter, close to 1.63 millimeters, is consistent with values reported for the Siberian sculpin Cottus volki, suggesting a conserved reproductive investment per offspring within this clade.

The maximum lifespan of Gymnocanthus detrisus has been estimated from otolith annuli analysis conducted on individuals collected from Alaskan continental shelf waters, where water temperatures average 7.6 °C [T = 7.6 °C]. Under these conditions, the oldest documented individuals reach approximately 16 years [am = approximately 16 years], an impressive longevity for a fish of at a temperature of 7.6 °C [T = 7.6 °C]this body size. This extended lifespan, combined with a relatively late age at first reproduction, suggests a slow life-history pace typical of high-latitude sculpins that experience pronounced seasonal fluctuations in food supply. The physiological mechanisms underpinning this longevity are not well understood, but may involve low routine metabolic rates and a reduced reliance on energetically costly burst swimming. Comparisons with congeneric species from warmer, more productive habitats suggest that temperature is a major determinant of the aging rate in this lineage.

Comparative analyses of body size and maturation schedules place Gymnocanthus detrisus among the larger-bodied members of its genus, with the female length at puberty of 18.8 centimeters [Lp = 18.8 centimeters] representing approximately 52 percent of the maximum ultimate total length of 36 centimeters [Li = 36 centimeters]. This proportional size at maturity is typical for cold-water cottids and reflects a life-history compromise between the benefits of early reproduction and the survival advantages conferred by continued somatic growth. The corresponding male length at puberty of 17.7 centimeters [Lp = 17.7 centimeters] indicates that males attain sexual maturity at a slightly smaller relative size, a pattern that may be linked to the energy demands of nest construction and egg guarding. These size thresholds, combined with the species' prolonged lifespan and high batch fecundity, position Gymnocanthus detrisus as a classic K-selected strategist within its benthic community.
